paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 05.11.2026. Petitioner by: M/s Asad Majeed Chaudhry, Ch. Zahid Majeed, Ch. Abdul Majeed, Ch. Ehsan ul Haq and Muhammad Waseem Arshad, Advocates. Nemo for respondents No.1 to 4. Respondents No.5,6 and 7 ex parte. MUHAMMAD SAJID MEHMOOD SETHI, J.- Through the instant revision petition, the petitioner has called in question the legality of order dated 18.11.2025 passed by the learned Senior Civil Judge, Sheikhupura, whereby his application under Order I Rule 10 CPC, seeking transposition from defendant No.1 to co-plaintiff in the pending suit for specific performance of agreement to sell, was dismissed.

Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant civil revision petition are that respondent No.1 instituted a suit for specific performance on 28.02.2024 on the basis of an agreement to sell dated 17.08.2023, allegedly executed pursuant to an earlier agreement dated 24.06.2022, concerning land measuring 17-Kanals 12-Marlas. The petitioner claims that respondentsNo.2 and 3 had earlier entered into an agreement to sell dated 06.04.2022, followed by another agreement dated 24.06.2022 in his favour against payment of Rs.2,20,00,000/-, and delivered possession of the property to him. Subsequently, an agreement dated 17.08.2023 was executed in favour of existing plaintiffs in the same chain of transactions. RespondentsNo.2 and 3, in their written statements, admitted execution of the preceding agreements, though disputed the petitioner's claim and the legal consequences flowing therefrom. During pendency of the suit, the petitioner filed an application under Order I Rule 10 CPC on 08.09.2025, seeking his transposition from defendant No.1 to a co-plaintiff, which was expressly consented to by respondents No.1 and 2. However, the learned Trial Court, vide order dated 18.11.2025, dismissed the application primarily on the ground that the petitioner had no direct privity of contract with respondentsNo.2 and 3 and had no enforceable title in the suit property, while observing that he could institute an independent suit for specific performance. Hence, the instant revision petition.

Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the impugned order has been passed without properly appreciating the successive transactions contractual arrangements and the interest acquired by the petitioner under the agreement dated 24.06.2022. He argues that respondents No.2 and 3, in their written statements, have admitted execution of the agreements dated 06.04.2022 and 24.06.2022, along with the relevant receipts, and therefore, the petitioner cannot be treated as a stranger to the transaction. He further contends that the subsequent agreement dated 17.08.2023 in favour of the existing plaintiffs was executed pursuant to the petitioner's earlier contractual arrangement and that both transactions concern the same property and forming part of interconnected contractual obligations. He maintains that the plaintiffs' express consent to the proposed transposition, coupled with the petitioner's direct interest in the subject matter, furnished sufficient grounds for allowing the application for his transposition as co-plaintiff. Reliance is placed upon Section 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and the judgment reported as Nisar Ahmed Afzal v. Muhammad Taj and 7 others (2013 SCMR 146).

The controversy requiring determination is the question whether the petitioner, being a party to the preceding agreement to sell dated 24.06.2022 and claiming an interest in the same property which forms the subject matter of the pending suit, could be transposed as a co-plaintiff under Order I Rule 10 CPC. It is important to clarify at the outset that the question of his ultimate entitlement to specific performance is, however, distinct from the question whether his presence in the proceedings, in the capacity sought, is necessary or appropriate for effectual and complete adjudication of the controversy.

A perusal of the record reveals that the successive agreements dated 06.04.2022, 24.06.2022 and 17.08.2023 relate to the same property measuring 17-Kanals 12-Marlas. The petitioner claims to have acquired contractual rights under the agreement dated 24.06.2022, whereas the existing suit has been instituted on the basis of the subsequent agreement dated 17.08.2023. Significantly, defendants No.2 and 3 have admitted execution of the preceding agreements, though disputing their legal consequences. Such admissions do not, by themselves, establish to the relief claimed; nevertheless, they constitute a relevant circumstance demonstrating that his asserted interest is rooted in the very chains of transactions which forms the factual foundation of the pending suit. His claim, therefore, cannot be dismissed at this preliminary stage as an entirely independent or extraneous controversy. These circumstances sufficiently demonstrate that the petitioner's claim is not wholly independent of, but intrinsically connected with, the controversy already pending adjudication.

The legal significance of successive agreements concerning immoveable property also requires consideration. An agreement to sell does not, by itself, create ownership or an interest in the property in the nature of title; nevertheless, it may confer enforceable contractual rights upon the purchaser. In this regard, Section 23 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, recognizes the right of a representative in interest to seek specific performance, subject to the exceptions contained therein. The august Supreme Court in Nisar Ahmed Afzal v. Muhammad Taj and 7 others (2013 SCMR 146) has also recognized the legal significance of successive agreements and the transfer of contractual benefits. Although an agreement to sell does not create ownership in immovable property, it may give rise to enforceable contractual rights. Thus, the absence of formal title in the petitioner or defendants No.2 and 3 could not, by itself, furnish a sufficient ground to reject the application without examining the nature and derivation of the alleged contractual interest.

The learned Trial Court primarily dismissed the application on the ground of absence of direct privity of contract between the petitioner and the contesting defendants. In this regard, the august Supreme Court in Nisar Ahmed Afzal v. Muhammad Taj and 7 others (2013 SCMR 146) has recognized that there is no legal bar to a prospective purchaser, holding rights under an agreement to sell, entering into a subsequent agreement to sell in respect of the same property. The said principle was also followed by this Court in Abdul Shakoor through Legal Heirs and others v. Rana Abid Mahmood and others (2025 YLR 229), wherein the legal efficacy of a subsequent agreement, executed pursuant to the authority conferred under the preceding agreement, was recognized. The aforesaid judicial pronouncements recognize that a person holding contractual rights under an agreement to sell is not, merely for want of formal transfer of proprietary title, precluded from entering into a subsequent contractual arrangement in respect of the same property, subject, of course, to the terms and legal effect of the underlying agreement. However, the distinction between assignment of contractual benefits and transfer of contractual obligations was also required to be examined in the light of the aforesaid judgment of the august Supreme Court. The learned Trial Court, without determining whether the petitioner's claim represented a lawful derivation of contractual rights or involved an impermissible transfer of contractual obligations, treated absence of direct privity as conclusive. Such an approach was not legally justified at the stage of deciding the application for transposition.

Another material consideration is that respondents No.1 and 2, being the existing plaintiffs, expressly consented to the petitioner's transposition. Although such consent cannot, by itself, bind the contesting defendants or establish the petitioner's substantive entitlement, it was a material consideration which deserved due weight. Moreover, the petitioner's proposed inclusion would enable the learned Trial Court to examine the interconnected agreements, consideration and respective contractual obligations in one proceeding, thereby avoiding unnecessary multiplicity of litigation and the possibility of conflicting findings.

The power under Order I Rule 10 CPC, however, is not unqualified. Transposition cannot be permitted merely because a person has some financial or collateral interest in the outcome of litigation, nor can it be employed to introduce an independent cause of action or transform the basic character of the suit. The proposed party must demonstrate a sufficiently direct and legally cognizable connection with the subject matter, and the proposed transposition must assist, rather than obstruct, adjudication of the existing lis. In the present case, the petitioner's claim arises from an earlier agreement concerning the identical property and forms part of the same sequence of contractual dealings upon which the existing suit is founded. His proposed inclusion, therefore, does not introduce an entirely foreign controversy or require adjudication of an unrelated cause of action. Rather, it would bring before the Court a person asserting contractual rights arising from the same series of transactions, whose claim may have a direct bearing upon the rights and obligations requiring determination in the pending suit.

The observation of the learned Trial Court that the petitioner may institute an independent suit does not adequately address the object and purpose of Order I Rule 10 CPC. The availability of an alternative remedy, by itself, is not a sufficient reason to exclude a person whose asserted rights are substantially interwoven with the controversy already pending adjudication. Procedural law is intended to advance the determination of substantive rights and not to multiply proceedings through an unnecessarily fragmented adjudication of interconnected disputes. Where the claims arise from the same property and successive contractual arrangements, their examination in one proceeding, subject to the rights of all parties to contest the same, is ordinarily conducive to judicial economy, consistency of findings and effective administration of justice. In the circumstances of the present case, the proposed transposition would preserve the existing foundation of the suit while enabling the Court to determine the interconnected contractual claims in the presence of the persons asserting rights thereunder.

Consequently, this Court is of the considered view that the learned Trial Court failed to properly appreciate the petitioner's asserted contractual interest, the admitted execution of the preceding agreements and the effect of the proposed transposition upon comprehensive adjudication of the controversy. The impugned order, therefore, suffers from material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in the learned Trial Court under Order I Rule 10 CPC, warranting interference under Section 115 CPC.

For the foregoing reasons, the instant revision petition is allowed. The impugned order dated 18.11.2025 is set aside and the petitioner's application under Order I Rule 10 CPC is accepted. The petitioner shall accordingly be transposed as a co-plaintiff, subject to consequential amendment of the plaint, if required, and affording the contesting respondents an opportunity to respond thereto. Needless to observe that all questions relating to the validity, enforceability and legal effect of the successive agreements, assignment of contractual rights and entitlement to specific performance shall remain open for determination by the learned Trial Court on the basis of evidence, without being influenced by any observation made herein. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge Approved for reporting Judge Waseem
